articles.title: As AI takes on more tasks, what happens when people have to jump in to clean up after it?
articles.author: Murugan Anandarajan, Professor of Decision Sciences and Management Information Systems, Drexel University
paras: Imagine an artificial intelligence system that has performed reliably for months. Its recommendations are almost always right, and the employee reviewing them has learned that close scrutiny rarely changes the outcome. Then something unusual happens. The AI makes an error or can’t proceed and needs human intervention. The employee is expected to step in and remains responsible for the outcome.
But does the employee know how to do the task?

I’m a professor of management information systems and the academic director of Drexel University’s Center for Applied AI & Business Analytics. In my research on human-AI relationships, I call this latent risk: the possibility that people may lose capabilities their organizations still depend on them to exercise.

AI can continue to perform well while the people overseeing it become less practiced at exercising independent judgment and less prepared to intervene. The risk becomes latent when the organization still depends on that human capability to step in but has little cause to notice that that capability may be weakening.

The concern is not entirely new. The idea of latent risk builds on decades of research into how people respond to automation. For example, studies of automation bias have shown that people can miss problems or follow automated recommendations even when other evidence suggests they should not.
What is different today is the role AI is beginning to play in organizations. It is beginning to assume larger parts of the analysis and decision-making that people previously performed.

The better AI becomes, the more the nature of human work changes. Work that once required an employee to analyze a problem and reach a decision may instead be performed by AI, leaving the employee to review its recommendation. The employee is no longer doing the same work with AI assistance – rather, their job has shifted from doing the work to overseeing what the AI does.

This shift is already beginning to change how some companies train employees. Accounting giant Deloitte, for example, is redesigning its graduate audit training as AI takes over some of the manual work traditionally done by junior auditors. The firm is introducing simulations so trainees can still develop the judgment they will need as they move into more complex work.

More than four decades ago, cognitive psychologist Lisanne Bainbridge described one of the “ironies of automation”: As systems take over more of the work, instead of simply having their work loads lightened, people can be left facing new challenges in monitoring the systems and handling the unusual situations the systems cannot. Later studies found another problem: As people become less involved in a task, they can become less prepared to step in when needed. Researchers have called this the out-of-the-loop performance problem.
This reduced involvement may affect more than a person’s readiness to intervene. It can change the capabilities available to the organization.

What work remains for people does not necessarily become easier. It may become harder. These are the situations where experience and independent judgment matter most. The result is a paradox: People may be called upon to exercise independent judgment less often, even as the judgments left to them become more difficult.
The accountability problem

Accountability may not change as quickly as the work does when organizations deploy AI systems. An employee may now oversee far more decisions than they make themselves, while remaining responsible for the outcomes. The organization’s expectations may still reflect how the work was divided before AI took on a larger role. The organization can therefore end up holding people accountable for decisions over which they have less control.

This creates a mismatch. Research on meaningful human control suggests that responsibility should match a person’s authority and ability to act. An employee may retain the authority to override an AI recommendation and remain responsible for the outcome, yet lose the capability to do so. Authority, responsibility and capability can begin to separate.
Latent risk becomes an organizational design problem, not simply a human performance problem.

Organizations typically judge AI-enabled processes by measures such as accuracy and productivity. Those numbers may look good even as the human role is changing. Suppose employees override AI recommendations less frequently over time. Is that a sign of growing dependence? Perhaps.

But it could also mean that the AI has become more accurate and there is less reason to intervene. The number of overrides alone tells little about whether employees remain ready to exercise their own judgment.

The key is to understand how the division of work between people and AI is changing. Which decisions have migrated from people to AI? What responsibilities remain with people? Looking at the performance of the employee or the AI separately may miss what is changing between them.
Organizational governance – defining roles and responsibilities – is also under pressure from AI.

Someone may remain formally in the loop with an AI system even as their actual role changes. Defining human and AI roles when a system is introduced is only a starting point. As AI improves and people become accustomed to using it, those roles are likely to change over time. There is nothing inherently wrong with that change.

The problem arises when the relationship changes but the assumptions surrounding it do not. It’s important for organizations to periodically ask: What relationship between people and AI did we design, and what relationship do we actually have today?
In short, organizational governance needs to be dynamic.
Maintaining the human backstop

Not every human capability needs to be preserved. If AI can perform a task well, there is little reason to require people to keep doing the same work. Organizations need to decide which capabilities they still expect people to have when human judgment is required. If people may still be called upon to use a capability, it needs to be maintained.

Overseeing AI is not the same as exercising independent judgment. If people rarely make the decision themselves, the organization cannot assume they will be ready when they need to. One way to test this is to occasionally ask employees to make a decision without first seeing the AI recommendation. The organization needs to know that the human backstop it relies on will actually work when needed.

As AI takes on more work, some human capabilities will inevitably be used less often. Some may no longer matter. Others may still be essential when AI reaches its limits. The challenge is knowing the difference and making that choice deliberately.
For me, the central question is this: Which human capabilities does an organization still depend on, and will they be there when needed?

articles.title: Is the world pricing the risk of a US diesel export ban?
articles.author: Michel Robe, Professor of Finance and Distinguished Chair, University of Richmond
paras: A spike in diesel prices is hammering broad sectors of the U.S. economy – especially agriculture and shipping – and becoming a flash point ahead of the November 2026 midterm elections.

This squeeze has prompted Republicans from hard-hit farm states to call for a ban on U.S. diesel exports, with President Donald Trump reportedly weighing the idea as well. He also announced a deal on Oct. 9 to supply Russian diesel to U.S. and global markets.
Meanwhile, the G7 countries have agreed to release an additional 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from their emergency reserves.

What would happen if the U.S. did enact an export ban? It’s a net exporter of petroleum products, so such a move would split the U.S. and world markets for diesel. The resulting mismatch between domestic demand and supply could depress U.S. diesel prices in the short term.

This would give some relief to American consumers, at least temporarily. But as a professor of finance who studies commodities and market volatility, I also see a big adverse shock hitting the rest of the world under that scenario.

The current political response to pricey diesel, however, shouldn’t be a surprise. A recent paper of mine, co-authored with two other economists, asks more broadly when governments are more inclined to restrict commodity exports. We found that export bans are more likely when prices are high and when politicians start weighing the preferences of commodity users, like consumers, over those of commodity producers, like the oil industry.
This could be what’s happening right now, amid record energy prices and just a few weeks from Election Day.

Diesel prices are hovering near all-time highs. The Energy Information Administration reports that the average price of the U.S. benchmark, known as ultra-low sulfur diesel, has topped US$7 per gallon in some regions like the West Coast.

Soaring energy prices are also continuing to push U.S. inflation up more broadly. Consumer prices in September jumped year-on-year by a higher-than-expected 3.7%, with gas prices responsible for more than half of the most recent monthly increase.

How did this happen? Before the conflict with Iran erupted in February 2026, key diesel exporters included Russia, Middle Eastern producers, the United States and China. Since then, those first two export sources have withered.

Russia, now in the fifth year of its war against Ukraine, banned diesel exports in July 2026 after Ukraine launched an effective air campaign that has knocked out more than half of Russia’s oil refinery capacity and destroyed many diesel storage-tank farms. That retaliatory campaign has pushed Russia from being a top diesel exporter to importing refined oil products, including diesel.

Meanwhile, in the Middle East, crude oil prices surged following missile attacks against Iran at the end of February. The Strait of Hormuz, which was the transit route for more than one-fifth of the global crude oil and natural gas output, essentially shut down amid fears over Iran targeting commercial ships sailing through.

Since then, increased shipments through Saudi and Emirati pipelines and actions by the U.S. Navy in the strait have helped restart petroleum flows. But the threat to Hormuz shipping remains real, as seen by recent strikes by Iranian forces on multiple tankers in early October.

These shocks have changed the economics of petroleum shipments in two ways. First, the price of transporting oil has more than quintupled, as tanker owners charge record fees to travel through the strait. Those fees, of course, bleed into the price that diesel buyers pay.

Second, in the strait, the content of tanker cargo has changed. Many ships are now loaded with crude oil, rather than diesel, after Iranian strikes on Gulf countries earlier this year knocked out a substantial share of the Middle Eastern refining capacity. Insofar as there isn’t much additional refinery capacity elsewhere in the world, even these restored crude oil flows can’t bring diesel prices down to prewar levels.
What an export ban would look like

The effects of removing Russian and Middle Eastern diesel from the market are being felt worldwide. One result is that U.S. diesel exports to the rest of the world have surged due to heightened foreign demand for the product and the high prices it can fetch abroad. Those export flows have been accompanied by the diesel price spike at home.

That jump in domestic prices is what’s driving discussions of a possible ban on U.S. diesel exports, and it reflects a dynamic that my co-authors and I laid out in our study of commodity export restrictions and bans. While we focused on agricultural markets, our findings also apply to the current diesel crunch.

Governments of commodity-exporting countries typically balance the interests of commodity producers and exporters, who prefer high prices, against those of domestic consumers, who like lower prices. When consumers’ wishes matter relatively more – for example, as elections approach – the likelihood of a ban rises.

American consumers never like high energy prices. Nowadays, after years of elevated inflation, they seem especially unhappy about them. Until the Iran war, Trump had been able to tout a substantial fall in petroleum product prices after he returned to office in January 2025. That’s no longer the case.

Higher diesel prices are being felt across the economy. The fuel is used to heat homes, especially in the Northeast, and to power machinery, tractors, trucks, boats and trains. This is why farmers and transportation operators are especially hard hit. Furthermore, these businesses typically try to pass their cost increases on to their customers. So shoppers are shelling out more for groceries and any other goods that must be transported.
Under the scenario of an export ban, the cost of U.S. diesel might fall in the short run, but world prices would spike. Soaring prices, however, would not be the only issue for the rest of the world.

Our research shows that a major exporting country’s ban would also increase market uncertainty and volatility. This is because restricting exports would effectively concentrate the rest of the world’s production, making the remaining supply base more fragile and increasing the rest of the world’s exposure to any subsequent output shocks.

If other countries think that their diesel situation is already bad, it would be much worse under a U.S. export ban. And the G7 move to release more diesel into the global market indicates that the rest of the world might understand how U.S. politics could lead to that outcome.

articles.title: What’s behind the BBC’s funding crisis? An expert explains
articles.author: Patrick Barwise, Emeritus Professor of Management and Marketing, London Business School
paras: In the run-up to the renewal of the BBC charter in January 2028, the corporation is facing perhaps its greatest ever funding crisis. It is staring down cost hyper-inflation across most programme genres and, unlike online-only streamers such as Netflix, it will still have to fund traditional broadcast networks until at least 2034. And of course, it will also have to pay for new digital services to keep pace with trends, especially among younger audiences.

But the biggest driver of the BBC crisis is the cut in real-terms funding for its national, regional and local UK services. These are the services that largely account for licence payers’ willingness to pay the fee.
The reduction in the real-terms funding of these services has been building up since 2010 and is now deeper than most people realise.

In 2010-11, TV licence fee revenue was £3.1 billion. The cost of collecting the licence fee was £124 million. The BBC also received £579 million of government funding from the Department for Work and Pensions for free TV licences for the over-75s.

So the total public funding from licence fees, after collection costs, and the DWP payment, was £3.5 billion. But not all of this went to the BBC: £80 million was “top-sliced” (or diverted) to meet the final costs of switching from analogue to digital TV.

By 2025-26, licence fee income had grown to £3.9 billion. But government support for free TV licences had been phased out and top-slicing increased to £293 million to fund the BBC World Service, BBC Monitoring (a division of the World Service), and the Local Democracy Reporting Service. The BBC was also partially funding the Welsh language TV channel S4C. That left the net public funding of its UK services at around £3.4 billion.

But between 2010 and 2025, the cumulative effect of inflation was 55.4%. This equates to a real-terms cut to public funding for the UK services of £2 billion per year – or put another way, a 37% drop in income.

Based on media coverage, you might think that the main reason for the BBC’s reduced income is that fewer people are paying the licence fee. But in reality, the 37% real-terms reduction was mainly driven by three other things.

First, successive governments were salami-slicing the value of the licence fee – in other words, repeated below-inflation settlements ate away at its value over time. Second, they withdrew government funding for free TV licences. Third, they more than doubled top-slicing in real terms, from £124 million to £293 million.
How BBC funding has fallen (figures in millions of pounds)

It’s true though that increases in licence fee evasion, from 5.2% in 2010-11 to 11.8% in 2025-26, played a part, as did the number of “no licence needed” households claiming that they did not need a TV licence because they “watch TV only on demand” but “never watch the BBC iPlayer”.

To put this into context, in 2015 99% of UK households used the BBC’s services in a single week. The figure may now be “only” 97% or 98%. But the idea that a large number are forced to pay without getting any direct benefit over a whole year seems implausible.
Many, however, take the BBC for granted – until they’re deprived of it. A study in 2022 found that after nine days without it, 70% of those who’d said it was poor value changed their minds.

To mitigate the cuts, the BBC has made continuous efficiency savings over the 15 years, reducing overhead costs, cutting staff and budgets, and squeezing suppliers. But, according to the National Audit Office, it now faces diminishing returns from these savings and most future cost-cutting will have to come from axed programmes, lower budgets and a reduction in the number of TV channels and radio stations. The axing of long-running Radio 4 consumer show You and Yours – along with other casualties – is a case in point.

The BBC also faces diminishing returns from commercial income, largely raised overseas from programme sales and format licences. With less investment in original content, quite simply the BBC now has less to sell.

The government says it wants to ensure sustainable BBC funding under the next charter. Achieving that will require updating or replacing the licence fee funding model, widening the payment base and bringing it closer to the BBC’s near-universal household usage. The financial stakes are surprisingly low: the £180 licence fee (with easy payment options) is equivalent to just £3.45 per week.

Limited, well-targeted exemptions for households for whom this is still a significant burden should be easily affordable, either for the government or for a properly funded BBC – even in the current fiscal situation. But as always, any policy that ends – or even reverses – the salami-slicing of BBC funding will be strongly opposed by its critics.

articles.title: Companies may be held liable when AI harms their clients and customers
articles.author: Sarah Webber, Associate Professor of Accounting, University of Dayton
paras: Artificial intelligence has moved quickly from a novelty on the job to a common workplace tool. Gallup found that 52% of U.S. employees and 68% of professional services workers were using AI by February 2026. Thomson Reuters similarly found in spring 2026 that 74% of professionals use AI several times a week for work.

This widespread use shouldn’t surprise anyone. For accountants, attorneys, consultants and other professionals, AI can accelerate research, summarize complex information and assist with writing and other forms of communication.

But its rapid adoption has a big downside – AI can produce information that sounds authoritative and looks polished while being completely wrong. And when AI generates mistakes, responsibility for those errors belongs to the professional or business relying on the AI output – not companies that develop AI systems.

AI errors have led to lawsuits, court fines, financial consequences and public embarrassment from fabricated citations, nonexistent sources and inaccurate AI-generated information. These cases raise an increasingly important question: How can professionals benefit from AI without outsourcing the judgment their work requires?

We are two certified public accountants who research tax accounting. In the September 2026 issue of Journal of Accountancy, we examined what happened in Clinco v. Commissioner, a case before the U.S. Tax Court where an attorney submitted a brief to the court with allegedly fake citations.

The Tax Court is a specialized federal court that resolves disputes between taxpayers and the IRS. This case involved a restaurant owner accused of underreporting more than US$2 million in business receipts and claiming unsupported depreciation deductions on rental properties. The main issue concerned Clinco’s accounting records used to determined how much of their income to tax.
The taxpayers’ attorney, Abraham Wagner, cited four cases to support his argument that an IRS notice assessing additional taxes was invalid.

The court determined that three of the citations appeared to be AI-generated hallucinations that cited nonexistent Tax Court cases. The court rejected the taxpayer’s argument and warned Wagner that submitting fake citations could lead to sanctions from the court, including financial penalties or disciplinary action against Wagner.
Ultimately, the court did not sanction Wagner in the case, but the decision stands to put attorneys and other professionals in Tax Court on notice that AI hallucinations will not be tolerated.
AI errors made on behalf of clients are not limited to briefs drafted by attorneys. Nor are these mishaps limited to the United States.

When Deloitte produced a 237-page report in 2025 for the Australian government examining its automated system for penalizing welfare recipients who failed to meet job-seeking requirements, it contained nonexistent academic citations and a fabricated quotation it attributed to a federal court judgment.
The global consulting firm later issued a revised version of the error-ridden report. Deloitte blamed generative AI for the errors in the original and agreed to partially refund its fees.

Like most airlines, Air Canada has a chatbot on its website to respond to its customers’ questions. The chatbot told a customer in November 2022 that he could buy a plane ticket under a bereavement policy and be reimbursed later. This was not company policy, and Air Canada refused to honor what the chatbot had told the customer.

The customer sued the airline and won 812 Canadian dollars in damages. The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal ruled that Air Canada had failed to take reasonable care to ensure that its AI bot provided accurate information and agreed with the customer that the airline had negligently misrepresented the bereavement policy.
There have been other lawsuits filed against AI platforms and providers.

In 2025, for example, a Georgia court dismissed a defamation lawsuit against OpenAI after its ChatGPT tool falsely accused Mark Walters, a radio host, of embezzlement. The court ruled in favor of summary judgment for OpenAI and found Walters had not established fault and damages.

There is also an ongoing case, Keene v. Google LLC, that is similar to the Walters case. Keene, a TV producer, sued after Google’s AI summaries allegedly published false information about Keene’s criminal history. In September 2026 the court ruled that some of his defamation claims may proceed, without deciding yet whether Google was liable.
Hallucinations and ‘confabulations’

Unfortunately, for anyone using AI to save time and use less labor, AI errors are often hard to spot. Unlike most obvious mistakes humans make, an AI-generated error may include supporting explanations, citations or references that make a passage appear complete and credible.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology issued a report on AI risk management in July 2024 that calls AI mistakes and hallucinations “confabulations” – the confident presentation of erroneous or false information.

Some researchers draw a more specific distinction between hallucinations, in which AI invents information outright, and confabulations, in which it fills gaps or distorts real information in a plausible way.
Either kind of problem can be hard to detect without independent verification, but confabulations mimic actual research so closely they can trick AI users into believing the AI output is valid.
AI errors in the workplace

A 2024 Stanford University study of specialized AI tools for legal research found erroneous results in 17% to 33% of the responses tested. Yet those findings and other grounds for concern about accuracy have not stopped many law firms from embracing AI tools due to their potential to save time and improve efficiency.

Recent surveys indicate law firms and other employers have not adopted enough workplace safeguards to spot and root out AI-generated mistakes. A 2026 survey by the Nationwide insurance company found that only 36% of surveyed businesses have written AI policies, and only 37% provide any training on responsible AI use.

As AI becomes more and more common in the workplace, we believe it’s clear that telling employees simply to “check the AI” is not enough. Businesses and the people working for them need clear expectations about when it’s appropriate to use AI, which outputs require independent verification, and who is ultimately responsible for the final work.
AI may change how professional work gets done, but it does not change where the buck stops.
The University of Dayton is an academic partner of The Conversation.
Kaitlin Newkirk is affiliated with the Ohio Society of CPAs.

articles.title: A crackdown on online shopping tricks is welcome, but doesn’t go far enough
articles.author: Nauman Wajid, Lecturer in Marketing, Birmingham City University
paras: Hurry! Only two left! Fourteen people bought this in the last hour! Fifty people are looking at this item!

Anyone who shops online will be familiar with these kinds of messages popping up on their screen. The online equivalent of a pushy salesperson, they are designed to create a sense of urgency around making a purchase.

These online tools are sometimes referred to as “dark patterns” – clever tricks built into apps and websites to encourage you to do things you may not necessarily want to do – like click the “buy” button. One large study revealed that over 11,000 shopping websites use these strategies.

For years this was seen as an inevitable – and irritating – part of online shopping. That’s beginning to change. The UK’s main consumer regulator, the Competition and Markets Authority, has been probing retailers on these very issues for the past few years.
And there have been noticeable successes against companies using misleading countdown timers and urgency claims, which they have since agreed to stop.
The CMA also has sharper teeth than before. Since April 2025, it has been given direct enforcement powers, including the ability to impose fines of up to 10% of a business’s worldwide turnover.
And there are new rules due in early 2027 on subscription contracts that will tackle practices such as pressure selling at renewals and hard-to-cancel subscriptions.
This is all real and meaningful progress.
The CMA is trying to track down deception. Was the countdown clock real or not? Was the previous price quoted ever actually charged?

But there is another effect of dark patterns that regulation doesn’t yet touch – what happens to you psychologically, after weeks, months, or years following the experience of being treated as the victim of these tactics, whether they’re technically accurate or not.
Research shows that scarcity cues, such as countdown timers, not only affect purchase decisions, but they also create a sense of time urgency and increased mental load on customers .

Studies have suggested a kind of emotional exhaustion, known as “digital burnout” that can occur due to heavy usage of digital consumer platforms, which are constantly fed to individuals via the algorithms they have developed.
Even a compliant, accurate countdown timer is designed to generate a sense of urgency and panic. A true “only two left” still makes you feel pressured.

My own ongoing research looks at the potential impact of AI-powered personalisation and nudging, which is getting more sophisticated every day. It is already becoming extremely adept at reading shoppers’ behaviour.
And this sort of pattern has been observed by researchers before. The psychological toll of constant algorithmic pressure is a distinct problem from whether or not a given claim is false.

The CMA can put an end to companies misinforming you on the matter of scarcity. It doesn’t have a way to correct for the effect over time of constant and accurate urgency messaging on stress levels or decision fatigue, which it’s not currently asked to address by the consumer protection law.
The question of whether something is true or not is one thing. But the effect that question has on consumers is an entirely separate issue that customers need to be aware of.

The CMA’s new powers give the regulator a credible deterrent that it did not have before. But they are yet to address the more complex and elements of dark patterns, which relate to how they actually make people feel.

articles.title: Councils that restrict harmful advertising won’t lose out on profits
articles.author: Kate Whitman, Research Fellow, University of Portsmouth
paras: For cash-strapped councils, turning away much-needed income by restricting adverts for junk food, fossil fuels or other harmful products might seem like a policy they can ill afford.
But a new report, published by the advocacy alliance Sustain and carried out by our team at the University of Portsmouth, suggests otherwise.

Our report found no evidence that councils introducing healthier food advertising policies lost advertising revenue when compared to places without such a policy. The finding held for councils across the UK with different advertising sites (from bus shelters to benches), locations and contract arrangements.

For our analysis, we sent freedom of information requests to all local councils in the UK. From the 360 responses received, only 38 councils provided enough data on the annual percentage change of revenue (between 2019-23) to allow for comparison. Three of those 38 councils had introduced healthier food advertising policies during that five-year period; the rest (35) did not have those policies.

By comparing the revenue of local governments that implemented a healthier food advertising policy to those without, a statistical model assessed whether council revenues were now below what would have been expected had they not implemented a healthier foods advertising policy. The findings show that councils did not lose potential revenue from implementing this policy.

Concern about lost income has been one of the practical arguments made against stronger advertising policies. Yet restricting harmful products does not mean leaving billboards and bus shelters empty. Advertising space can instead be filled by more socially beneficial campaigns, such as healthy products, while companies affected by the rules can switch to promoting products that comply with them.

This can also reduce the financial pressure on other public services. Transport for London’s restrictions on advertising foods high in fat, salt and sugar have been associated with households purchasing around 1,000 fewer calories from unhealthy foods each week. Modelling of the policy estimated that resulting health benefits could save the NHS and social care system £218 million over the lifetime of the current population.
Now councils are beginning to apply the same thinking beyond junk food.

Public bodies are extending the principle already applied to tobacco, alcohol and unhealthy food to fossil fuels and other high-carbon products: that publicly controlled advertising space should not be used to promote forms of consumption that undermine public health or environmental goals.

More than a dozen UK councils including Sheffield and Edinburgh have adopted some form of restriction on high-carbon advertising, covering products and services such as fossil fuels, flights and non-electric cars.
And the boundaries continue to expand.

Bristol City Council recently became the first UK council to restrict advertising for ultra-fast fashion (brands that launch new designs on a daily or weekly not seasonal basis, leading to accelerated overproduction and waste) on council-owned sites, alongside new curbs on promoting fossil fuels, SUVs, airlines and cruises. The move brings an industry associated with high levels of production, consumption and waste within the scope of councils’ environmental advertising policies.

In another UK first, Portsmouth City Council included single-use plastics in its list of restricted products, alongside fossil fuels, non-electric cars and unhealthy food. Their inclusion signals a recognition of the environmental costs of disposable plastic packaging – and that an advert for a product packaged in single-use plastic is, in effect, an advert for both.

These decisions point towards a change in thinking. By expanding policies to include ultra-fast fashion and single-use plastics, UK councils appear to be recognising a wider range of environmental harms associated with the products advertised in public spaces, from the resources used to produce them to the waste they leave behind.
It also raises a broader question about whether council-owned advertising space should encourage forms of consumption that conflict with councils’ own commitments on public health, climate and waste.

However, developments outside the UK suggest this approach could go further. In May, Amsterdam became the first capital city to introduce legally binding restrictions on public advertising for fossil-fuel products and services. Those include flights, cruises and petrol and diesel cars, as well as meat. The inclusion of meat extends restrictions beyond products directly associated with fossil fuels to another major source of consumption-related environmental impacts.

The question for UK councils, then, is not simply whether these policies work, but how much further they are prepared to go. Until now, the prospect of losing advertising income has provided an economic argument for caution. Our new research weakens that argument.

If local authorities can set stronger standards without sacrificing advertising revenue, they have more room to align their advertising estates with the public health and environmental goals they are already spending money to achieve.

The shifts in both Bristol and Portsmouth show that the boundaries of acceptable advertising are already shifting in the UK. The evidence from our new report suggests councils may be able to afford to be bolder about where those boundaries are drawn.
Kate Whitman was a research consultant to Sustain for this project.

articles.title: Social Security benefits will rise 3.6% in 2027, but that may not be enough to offset healthcare costs
articles.author: Pankaj Agrrawal, Professor of Finance, University of Maine
paras: Monthly checks for the nearly 76 million Americans who receive Social Security benefits will rise by 3.6% in 2027. The increase, announced on Oct. 14, 2026, is the largest since the one that took effect in 2023.

This cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, is how the government tries to make sure that the value of Social Security benefits keeps up with inflation. Without it, the same payment would cover less of what recipients are spending on medical care, housing, groceries, clothing and other necessities.

I am a finance professor, and one of the topics I research is how inflation affects retirees’ investment choices. And I believe the upcoming bump doesn’t capture the inflation challenges that many people who receive Social Security benefits face.

The percentage increase in Social Security benefits depends in part on the annual inflation rate as of September 2026. It stood at 3.7% that month, as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a government agency, also announced on Oct. 14.

But the size of the increase is only part of the issue. The index used to set the COLA reflects what working people buy, not retirees, and that is a mismatch at the heart of a long-running debate over how the adjustment should be measured.

The government has annually increased Social Security benefits to keep up with inflation since 1975. Congress previously had to pass a law each time it increased benefits. As a result, years could pass without an adjustment, despite climbing prices.

The metric that the government uses is its consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers, known as the CPI-W. The Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks changes in the prices of goods and services that working households typically buy to calculate this index.

The Social Security Administration then compares the average CPI-W reading for July, August and September with the average for those same months in the prior year to set the COLA adjustment, which kicks in the following January.
If the economy contracts and prices fall, however, benefits stay the same. That happened in 2009, 2010 and 2015.
Spending much of the bump on premiums
One big problem with this calculation is that it understates healthcare inflation.

Out-of-pocket health costs, including Medicare premiums, deductibles and copayments for medical care and prescription drugs, typically consume nearly 30% of Social Security benefits, according to research from the nonpartisan Center for Retirement Research at Boston College.

For example, the government deducts Medicare Part B premiums directly from many retirees’ Social Security checks. The standard monthly Part B premium rose by US$17.90 in 2026, from $185 to $202.90. That increase alone consumed roughly one-third of the average $56 monthly gain in benefits from the 2026 COLA.

More broadly, this big jump in healthcare costs for people covered by Medicare, as most Americans getting Social Security benefits are, helps explain why there is a long-running debate over how the program measures inflation.

Critics of the system the government uses to adjust benefits for inflation, including the Senior Citizens League and the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, say the CPI-W reflects the spending habits of working people, who shell out less on medical care than retirees. Retirees also tend to spend less on clothing, education and transportation than people with jobs.

There are other ways the government measures inflation, including the consumer price index for Americans 62 and older, known as the CPI-E, that could be more accurate. The Bureau of Labor Statistics began to calculate this experimental index in the 1980s, but the Social Security Administration has not used it to set benefits yet despite some efforts in Congress to make the switch.

The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare has researched how much more older people spend on medical care. People 65 and older spend more than twice as much as younger Americans on out-of-pocket health and medical costs, the group estimates.

Those 75 and older spend nearly three times as much, the committee estimated after reviewing data from 1982 through 2014. It argues that a CPI-E weighted more toward medical care, housing and recreation would yield slightly larger cost-of-living adjustments than the CPI-W.

But an index tied to how older people generally spend their money does not always lead to a bigger cost-of-living adjustment. The CPI-E has increased less than CPI-W in some years. What’s more, the CPI-E was not designed to set benefits and would need a larger survey sample before it could be used for that purpose.
This article was originally published on Oct. 13, 2026. It has been updated with the latest cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security benefits.

articles.title: Americans are stressed about grocery prices, so why do they toss or overlook so much ‘misfit’ food?
articles.author: Jintao Zhang, Assistant Professor of Marketing, Binghamton University, State University of New York
paras: There’s a paradox that drives the shopping decisions of many Americans: Almost three-quarters say they’re feeling stressed out about skyrocketing grocery bills. But they keep discarding large quantities of food that’s safe to eat, from crooked carrots to surplus yogurt to “best before” items pulled from shelves early.

Overall, the U.S. government estimates that 30% to 40% of all food – from consumers, retailers and producers – is thrown out. That’s not just a massive missed opportunity for people experiencing food insecurity, but it’s also a significant contribution to global warming. According to the United Nations, 8%-10% of carbon emissions globally result from food waste.

In recent years, however, a market to rescue discarded groceries and repurpose food scraps and by-products has grown dramatically. This ranges from marketing “ugly” produce to appeal to more consumers to upcycling food by-products.

I study how consumers evaluate product value and quality, and my research suggests that American shoppers are much less fixated on prices or environmental impact. Instead, they care about quality. Even when perfectly good “misfit” produce is deeply discounted, for example, many shoppers assume that the low price reflects poor quality and either walk away or reach for a fruit or vegetable they think looks better.

What does this mean for reducing food waste and shedding these purchasing biases? My research has found that smarter and more effective labeling can make a big difference. A discount or promise of lower carbon emissions isn’t enough by itself – people have to believe the food is good first.
Making ‘ugly’ food attractive

A whole retail sector is now dedicated to marketing misfit food. “Ugly produce” delivery companies like Hungry Harvest and Misfits Market are rescuing and reselling food to shoppers who want to save and reduce their carbon footprint. Misfits Market alone has rescued more than 265 million pounds (about 120 million kilos) of food since 2018 and sells it at an average discount of 35%.

Another example is Too Good To Go, an app that sells “surprise” bags of surplus food at about one-third of the retail price. It estimates that it has saved more than 26 million meals, including through partnerships with more than 530 Whole Foods stores. And the app Flashfood encourages grocers to list meat, dairy and produce nearing their best-before date at around half price and directs shoppers, including those on public food assistance, to those deals.

Consumers appear to be responding. Too Good To Go users in the U.S. saved 8.1 million meals in the first seven months of 2025, a 67% jump from the year before, while Misfits Market rescued 27 million pounds of food (about 12 million kilos) in 2025, up from 23 million (about 10 million kilos) in 2019, its first full year of operation.

This market is also using smarter labeling to grow its appeal. Shoppers who believe that food appearance is important tend to judge misshapen produce as lower quality. But labeling these offerings as “ugly” actually reduces that bias because it signals that the only flaw is cosmetic. Another study found that in-store messages that raise shoppers’ self-esteem can also make a different: In field tests, a “Different Outside. Same Inside” message successfully urged people to overlook external appearance when making judgments, whether on people or food.

This sustainability push is also playing out in the processed and semi-processed foods market, where would-be waste is converted into upcycled products. Examples include flour milled from soybean pulp, snacks that leave the fruit peel on, and “bites” made from rescued bananas.

Companies that want to market these goods can get third-party certification through Upcycled Certified if they pass an audit of their supply chain. More than 600 products from over 100 brands now carry it, and sales of certified products grew 17% from 2024 to 2025.

Here, too, perceptions of quality matter. In research on consumers’ acceptance of these foods, my co-authors and I found that they made their purchase decision based largely on whether they believed the product was as good as its conventional counterpart.

But in this case, in contrast to “ugly” produce, these products tend to be pricier, so they can’t compete through discounting. Rather, they usually sell at a premium – like this small bag of specialty flour going for $7. That means that it’s even more important they signal higher quality so they can appeal to less price-constrained shoppers.

Generational attitudes differ on this point, our research found. Gen Z, millennials and baby boomers are more willing to buy foods certified as upcycled if they agree that the quality and environmental appeal are worth it. But Gen Xers – those who were born between 1965 and 1979 – show less enthusiasm, citing a perception of lower quality.

That result fits what we generally know about Gen X shoppers. We discovered they are hard to persuade and cost-conscious, and they tend to rely much more on their own judgment. Gen Xers are also least likely to eat out or go shopping for groceries online, preferring instead to cook for themselves. That means they tend to scrutinize foods more closely in the store.
A “green” benefit won’t beat these skeptics. They need an assurance of quality from brick-and-mortar retailers they trust, rather than from online platforms.

The encouraging news from our research is that it sometimes doesn’t take much to change beliefs. In two experiments, my co-authors and I tested whether a simple logo could shift shoppers’ perceptions of foods made from rescued ingredients. We designed one version that was round, green and descriptive, following established design principles: Circular logos signal higher quality, while descriptive ones lift brand evaluations. The other was hexagonal, monochrome and bare.

We found that shoppers who saw products with the well-designed logo rated those foods higher in quality and were more willing to buy them than those who saw the same products with no logo. The poorly designed logo, meanwhile, made no difference.

It was the increase in perceived quality, in our view, that made people more willing to buy. A logo that looks credible, explains itself and signals care can change what shoppers believe. A forgettable one might as well not be there.

Closing this gap in perceptions, in short, doesn’t require shoppers to care more about the planet. It requires them to believe the food is good. The rescue economy can make that case, but it has to lead with quality and not only with conscience.

articles.title: What colleges and universities need from donors to thrive
articles.author: William Blomquist, Professor Emeritus of Political Science, Indiana University
paras: In 1638, John Harvard, an English-born Puritan minister and teacher in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, bequeathed 400 books and half his £779 estate, today equivalent to roughly US$2 million, to the college that would be renamed in his honor after his death.

In addition to launching America’s oldest university, Harvard’s donation began a tradition of philanthropy for U.S. colleges and universities that has continued ever since. Today, philanthropy is an important source of higher education funding that covers an average of 10% of college and university budgets.

Based on our decades of experience as scholars, academic administrators and school fundraisers, we believe that donors – and not just big ones – are especially important to colleges and universities in tough times.

Since January 2025, the Trump administration has targeted colleges and universities with research funding cuts, student financial aid caps and new restrictions on how long international students can stay in the United States.

University endowments have been in the crosshairs since the first Trump administration’s 2017 tax reform package. The big 2025 tax-and-spending package Trump signed raised the taxes on some schools’ endowments. A rule the Trump administration proposed in September 2026 would threaten private schools’ tax-exempt status if any of their programs use race-based criteria.
There are demographic problems too. Fewer students are choosing to go to college, and the number of high school graduates who could attend is falling due to a declining birthrate.
Although colleges and universities are providing more financial aid than ever, students and their families are still struggling to pay for college.

Some schools are being forced to close their doors. Sixteen colleges shut down in 2025 alone, including Indiana’s only predominantly Black college, Martin University, and ecologically focused Sterling College in Vermont.
And at least 40 colleges have been acquired by other schools since 2020, including Marymount Manhattan College and Mills College, which are now part of Northeastern University’s global network.
Donors contributed $79 billion to colleges and universities in 2025, up 4% in constant dollars from the year before.
The richest Americans dominate giving to higher education: 89% of the funds raised came from only 2% of donors in 2025.

Also in 2025, Phil and Penny Knight, the Nike co-founder and his wife, made what was then the largest single gift to a university in history when they gave the Oregon Health & Science University $2 billion for cancer research.
On Sept. 30, 2026, investor Ken Griffin broke that record by giving Carnegie Mellon University more than $3 billion to build a new campus in Miami and meet some other priorities.

It’s hardly the only megagift a university has received in 2026: Michael and Susan Dell, whose fortune comes from his computer hardware company, gave the University of Texas at Austin $750 million for its medical center. The Knights gave $1 billion to the University of Oregon for a new engineering college. Software billionaire David Duffield pledged $371 million to Cornell University. And many other schools have drawn gifts in excess of $100 million.

The vast majority of these huge gifts are reserved for specific purposes. The share of totally unrestricted gifts to colleges and universities, those given with no strings attached, has been dwindling for decades. In 2024 it slipped below 7%. Unrestricted giving did pick up somewhat in 2025. Perhaps that was a sign that some donors were responding to federal funding cuts with their gifts.

In an article in Change: The Magazine of Higher Learning in September 2026, we listed ideas for college and university fundraising efforts. These tie to three recommendations for donors – and not only those making multimillion-dollar gifts.
Donations to colleges and universities don’t have to end in lots of zeros to make a big difference.

In 2015, the grassroots Saving Sweet Briar campaign kept the small women’s college operating even after its trustees had voted to close it. The largest gift the rural Virginia school received was $2 million, and the smallest was $1.50 from a graduate’s grandchild. This is the exception rather than the rule. Financial pressures were too much for Hampshire College, a New England private college that is slated to close after the fall semester of 2026, to withstand – even with a fundraising campaign and $5 million gift from alum and documentary filmmaker Ken Burns.

Giving Days are high-profile fundraising campaigns through which many alumni and other supporters raise millions. For example, Oregon State University Dam Proud Day 2026 drew 12,400 gifts and raised over $4.1 million. Purdue University’s annual “day of giving” has generated nearly $500 million over the past decade. In 2024, it garnered $76 million from 32,000 donors.
2. Donating with few or no strings attached
Donations with few restrictions or none at all help colleges and universities meet their greatest needs.
Even if they’re mostly intended for a new building or to fund a particular program, large gifts can also include unrestricted portions to help cover costs as needs arise and priorities change.

Brandeis University, Indiana University, Princeton University and other schools encourage unrestricted annual gifts. These flexible funds are helping to cover research funding shortfalls at Cornell University, undergraduate scholarships at Georgetown University and general operations at the College of the Atlantic.

Novelist and philanthropist MacKenzie Scott, the former wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, has given more than $26 billion in unrestricted donations to nonprofits, including to colleges and universities. Historically Black colleges and universities as well as other schools with diverse student bodies, such as Robeson Community College in rural North Carolina, Oklahoma’s Carl Albert State College and Wisconsin’s Fond du Lac Tribal and Community College, have received Scott’s big gifts.

In 1920, the trustees of Berea College, a private liberal arts school in Kentucky, passed a resolution placing future unrestricted bequests, donations made through people’s estates, in the school’s endowment. Berea students do not pay for tuition, fees, housing or food – thanks in large part to those unrestricted donations.
3. Helping students afford all college costs so they can graduate
Supporting students directly helps them go to college, stay in school and graduate.

Donors already make gifts that fund schools’ financial aid packages, with about $7 billion in gifts designated for this purpose in 2025. But the colleges and universities that receive the most dollars from donors serve a small fraction of the nation’s undergraduate students – and not those from low-income families. We recommend that donors consider making gifts to the thousands of colleges and universities, including community colleges, that don’t typically draw big donations and have endowments totaling in the millions, rather than billions, of dollars.

Sometimes it takes more than tuition scholarships for students to graduate. Donors can pay for additional expenses, such as transportation and textbooks, and fund extra academic advising and mentoring. Billionaire philanthropists John and Laura Arnold’s Commit2Completion grant program at Arizona’s Maricopa Community Colleges addresses those kinds of often overlooked priorities.

You don’t have to be very wealthy to fund scholarships. Anyone can pitch in through platforms like Dollars for Scholars. This program’s more than 400 chapters enable local donors to pool their gifts to help students raised in their communities pay college expenses. For example, a rural Minnesota chapter awarded $248,000 to 65 college-bound students in 2025.

There are also hundreds of other place-based “promise programs” that provide tuition and fees scholarships to public colleges and universities in their areas and offer programming such as college readiness workshops and access to local employers.

Philanthropy can’t solve every problem higher education faces. But by giving together, donating with fewer strings attached and helping students pay their college expenses, alumni and other donors can be strategic in how they help.
Genevieve Shaker has received funding from the TIAA Institute and the AFP Foundation for Philanthropy.

articles.title: Turmoil within Dolly Parton’s estate underscores the precariousness of family businesses after founders die
articles.author: Reid Kress Weisbord, Distinguished Professor of Law, Rutgers University - Newark
paras: Dolly Parton’s nephew Bryan Seaver announced the legendary singer’s death on Aug. 25, 2026, in a prerecorded video. Seaver, the son of one of Parton’s 11 siblings, had been her head of security for many years.
But Seaver is currently embroiled in a messy dispute with She’s Alive LLC, the company Parton established to manage her business assets after her death.
This unusually acrimonious fight highlights some of the business succession problems that can arise when the founder of a company dies but wants its other leaders to keep it going.
Parton, a legendary American singer, actress, entrepreneur and philanthropist, left behind an estimated US$450 million estate.

She’s Alive LLC terminated Seaver’s involvement with the business, and a court has issued a restraining order against him. Seaver is accused of engaging in “an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats” against Parton’s estate. He denies the allegations.

As professors who research and teach topics related to inheritance law, we are fascinated by the Parton case. It illustrates some of the pitfalls of planning for the transition of a privately held business after the founder’s death – a concern for celebrity and noncelebrity estates alike.
Managing celebrity estates after death

Celebrity estates, like Parton’s, are distinct because they often contain valuable intellectual property. This includes copyrights, which protect creative works, such as songs and recordings, including Parton’s catalog of hits. Another valuable asset in these estates are publicity rights, which protect the use of the celebrity’s name or likeness, such as the use of Parton’s face on a T-shirt sold for profit.

These rights can be enormously valuable long after the celebrity has died. Without careful planning beforehand and appropriate management after death, the estate may never get the full value of these property interests.

Prince, for example, died in 2016 without a will or any formal estate plan. The twice-divorced Minneapolis pop star had no surviving children. His estate passed to his siblings, who were his sole heirs.

It took more than six years to administer his complicated $156 million estate, which concluded with the heirs establishing corporate entities to manage his intellectual property rights. One of those entities, Prince Legacy LLC, recently became embroiled in litigation when some of Prince’s heirs sought to fire the managers who had been hired to manage their share of the intellectual property rights.

Marilyn Monroe, who died in 1962, also without any children, left behind a professionally drafted will under which her longtime acting coach, Lee Strasberg (and his then-wife) inherited most of her publicity rights. But Strasberg remarried, and his widow – a woman whom Monroe never met – hired various professional managers, including a company known as CMG Worldwide, which specializes in the management, marketing and promotion of publicity rights associated with dead celebrities.
Because of the successful management of her estate’s publicity rights, Monroe became known as one of the highest-paid dead celebrities – with large sums enriching a woman she’d never met.
Should a founder’s relatives remain in charge?
Many much-less famous family businesses face similar questions about how to keep their profits and revenue flowing and who should manage the company after the founder of a family business dies.

A continuation of business operations may have many benefits for a deceased founder’s family. The founder may have relayed their succession plans to them. Relatives often have institutional knowledge and loyalties that can enhance the value of the business and make it last longer.
Studies have not conclusively shown, however, whether continuing a business within the family is clearly better or worse for its bottom line than having outsiders manage it.

As one study found, family managers often have a “sense of kinship obligation” and enjoy “personal and social fulfillment” from working together in the business. That, in turn, creates incentives to manage the firm carefully with an eye toward long-term survival.
By contrast, another study of small and medium-size businesses after the sudden death of a CEO-owner found that, in the short run, nonfamily successors are better equipped to run the company.

Relatives, by contrast, may be hampered by grief and the emotional impact of the death. But the study also found that in the long run, family members may be more successful in managing the business because they “are likely to view the firm’s survival as a way to stay connected with the deceased family member and keep their memory alive. In turn, this is expected to inspire great stewardship towards the firm.”

Other studies, however, have found that maintaining family control over the management of a company after its founder’s death can hurt its performance. Restricting the pool of potential managers to relatives excludes better-qualified candidates who can bring expertise and experience that members of the family lack. Research has shown that hiring pros tends to be best for the business.
Death can be bad for business

When the owner of a privately held business dies, their assets, including real property, intellectual property and investments, will pass to others according to the estate plan, if the owner created one.
But in many cases, the true value of a business is more than just the sum of all its assets. Some of the value may reside in the owner’s talent, knowledge and business acumen.

In some cases, the owner maintained personal relationships with employees or customers that may have played a key operational role. In others, the owner may have relied upon unique personal qualities to achieve success in business. Parton herself, for example, was likely the most significant driver of value for her business because of her creativity and star power.
According to a 2022 study by economists who studied what happened to startups following the death of nearly 1,500 business founders, growth and profitability fell after the founder’s death.
Smaller companies are at risk of having to close altogether.

The study found that the negative effects on business continuity “appear to be driven by entrepreneur specialness rather than leadership transition,” which suggests that the founder’s unique contributions to the business can be difficult to replicate after death even with excellent transition planning.
What this means for Parton’s estate

Parton’s full estate plan is not yet publicly known, but she did not have any children, and her husband died before her. According to court filings, Parton engaged in “extensive estate planning measures” that included trusts and various corporate entities to manage her business assets and intellectual property rights.

She gave generously to charity, with acclaimed gifts for medical research and disaster relief. She also created the Imagination Library through her Dollywood Foundation. It sends free books to millions of children from their birth until their fifth birthday.

The amount that anyone – family, friends or charities – will receive from the estate of a wealthy celebrity depends on how their business assets and intellectual property rights are managed after death. Parton planned carefully, but it is up to others to make the most of what she left behind.

articles.title: Economics Nobel: how this year’s winners helped to smooth the cycle of economic peaks and troughs
articles.author: Conor O'Kane, Senior Lecturer in Economics, Bournemouth University
paras: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has awarded this year’s Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences to the American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford. The prize was awarded in recognition of their development of macroeconomic models that helped to reduce the length and depth of economic downturns.

According to the Academy, the economists’ work in macroeconomic modelling has given policymakers additional tools to smooth out the economic cycle. As well as reducing the severity of downturns, their work also helped to cool the potentially negative impacts of economic booms.

Economies are known to follow cycles of downturns and upturns – and economists have long sought to find ways to tame these. More than a century ago, British economist John Maynard Keynes developed an approach to managing the economy that came to be known as Keynesianism.

Before this, the classical “laissez-faire” approach dominated. According to this doctrine, in an economic downturn, markets would eventually clear and the economy would rebound. Any attempt by government to directly influence the economy would not work and could even make things worse.

Keynes disagreed with the classical view. He believed that economies could get locked into a downward spiral that would deepen recessions and lead to economic depression. Instead, he argued that governments could actively use the levers of monetary policy (adjusting interest rates) and fiscal policy (lowering taxes and government spending) to improve the health of the economy.

In the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street crash, the US was in a deep economic depression. Franklin D. Roosevelt won a landslide presidential victory in 1932 and his “New Deal” approach to economic policy was similar to what Keynes advocated. The US economy recovered, and the Keynesian school would dominate policymaking in many advanced economies after the second world war.

But the oil crisis of the 1970s changed everything. The Keynesian approach was ineffective in dealing with low growth, spiralling inflation and high unemployment. Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher won elections in the US and UK with promises of “smaller government” economic policy, including lower taxes, privatisation and deregulation. Keynesianism needed a rebuild.
Decisions of consumers and businesses

Hall and Woodford became part of the “New Keynesian” school that emerged in the 1980s. Their approach was to build models that looked at decisions made by millions of individuals and businesses rather than just considering macroeconomic variables like production, inflation, consumption and unemployment.

Hall, of Stanford University in California, is an expert in consumption theory. According to his “random walk hypothesis”, decisions made by households on whether to spend or save were directly influenced by their expectations about future income and economic conditions. In other words, they were not just based on their current financial conditions. As consumption makes up around 70% of GDP in advanced economies, these insights were important.

Woodford, of Columbia University in New York, is an expert in supply-side macroeconomics, specifically the role that expectations play in price-setting and inflation. In his 2003 book, Interest and Prices: Foundations of a Theory of Monetary Policy, he proved that a central bank could influence economic activity by managing the public’s expectations about what might happen to interest rates in future.

Up until the 1990s, central bank policymaking was secretive and could sometimes take markets by surprise. Hall and Woodford’s insights changed this. In the aftermath of the 2008 global financial crisis, the central banks of most major advanced economies adopted an approach known as “forward guidance”.

This policy saw central bank governors provide greater transparency about their monetary policy intentions. Forward guidance policy announcements provide a clear assessment of both the economic outlook and how this might affect inflation. They also set out how central bank policy could react to these assessments.

As with most policy approaches, forward guidance has both advocates and critics. Research from the European Central Bank shows that clear communication from central banks reduces short-term interest rate volatility. There is also some evidence that after the 2008 financial crisis, expectations that inflation would remain low helped to keep interest rates down. This probably encouraged spending and investment, which aided economic recovery.

But critics believe that forward guidance has no impact on long-term interest rates and say it is debatable if it has any impact on short-term rates. They also argue that setting expectations about interest rates can strip credibility from central banks. This could happen if economic policy needs to be altered to deal with sudden shocks, for example.

The conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine are driving up energy prices and inflation expectations. The forward guidance from many central bankers is pointing to higher inflation and perhaps the need for higher interest rates.

Anyone coming off a fixed-rate mortgage might be sceptical of the idea that policy tools can lower short-term interest rate expectations. This is not to say that Hall and Woodford’s work has not been transformative. But economies are difficult beasts – and debates around central bank policymaking are sure to continue.

articles.title: Unpicking the pensions triple lock: where it came from, and what might happen next
articles.author: Maria Evandrou, Professor of Gerontology, University of Southampton
paras: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has made the politically risky decision to adjust the pensions triple lock from April 2030.

Speaking at this year’s Labour Party Conference, he said: “Some may not realise it but older people with nothing more than the state pension, or only a little more, can find themselves paying care charges today from that small income. Under my plan, this will no longer happen.”
But what is the triple lock, and why was the announcement so controversial?

The triple lock is a mechanism that provides a guaranteed increase in the basic and new state pension. It raises it by whichever is highest among average earnings growth, price inflation, or 2.5% and ensures that state pension payments increase in value every April.

Politicians have long considered any challenge to the triple lock to be highly risky to their chances at the ballot box. But how long has the mechanism been in place and what were the reasons for its introduction?

Increasing the value of pensions has been hotly debated since the early 1970s. Back then, the Labour government introduced legislation to increase long-term benefits and state pensions in line with earnings or prices, whichever was higher – a “double lock” on pensions growth.

But by the late 1970s, the governing Conservative party deemed this mechanism “unsustainable” because of the same “ratchet effect” that the triple lock is now criticised for. In other words, for the rest of the population, their wages grew in response to inflation – but pensioners enjoyed the rise every year. Pensions were then linked to prices only, rather than slower-growing earnings.

During the 1980s and 1990s, concerns grew about a growing number of people falling into poverty in later life. Consecutive governments debated whether the link to earnings should be restored. At the same time, pensioners were experiencing a steady decrease in the value of the state pension relative to average earnings. This went from a peak of 26% of average earnings in 1979 to around 16% of average earnings between 2000 and 2010.

In 1999, there was a reckoning when pensioners received an increase of just 75p per week after a period of low inflation. The tiny uptick sparked anger and then-chancellor Gordon Brown was under pressure to act. Finally, in 2002, the Labour government legislated to increase pensions by the higher of 2.5% or price inflation. The double lock was back in place.

A key point came when the (first) Pensions Commission in 2005 published its recommendation that the government restore the link of pensions with earnings. This was a bid to reduce the risk of pensioners falling into poverty and placing pressure on the system of means-tested benefits.

This recommendation was followed by the announcement of a triple lock by the Conservative/Liberal Democrat coalition government in its first budget in 2010. It had been a key promise in the Lib Dem manifesto, and it was implemented in 2011 by then-chancellor George Osborne.

Since 2011, the triple lock has increased the value of the state pension considerably. Analysis by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) showed that between 2010-2023, the median disposable household income for pensioners rose by 15%. Cross-party support for maintaining the triple lock during the 2019 general election demonstrated a broad commitment to the steady increase of the state pension.

However, while average incomes in later life have risen, the gap between poorer pensioners and those on average incomes has widened. Relative poverty among pensioners rose from 13% in 2011, to 16% in 2022. Thus, the triple lock has not necessarily meant that fewer? pensioners are living in poverty.

At the same time, the key safety net for low-income pensioners is not the state pension alone. Historically, this was provided by something called the minimum income guarantee. This is a means-tested benefit which ensures that pensioners’ weekly income does not fall below a legally set minimum (£238 per week for a single person in 2026/7, and £363.25 for a couple), which was also linked to earnings.

The minimum income guarantee was replaced by the guarantee element of pension credit (a means-tested benefit that tops up the income of poorer pensioners). This move towards some kind of guarantee of a minimum income didn’t come with the fanfare of the triple lock – but it did make a big difference to pensioners’ incomes before the triple lock was introduced.

The Resolution Foundation, an independent thinktank focused on raising UK living standards, estimated that there was a 15.8 percentage point fall in pensioner relative poverty between 1997-98 and 2011-12, as growing incomes for poor pensioners closed the gap with the non-pensioner median income.
But there are still an estimated 760,000 vulnerable pensioners who are eligible for means-tested pension credit, but who failed to claim it in 2025/6.

The government’s own analysis shows that this happens for a number of reasons: people may not have heard of it, or don’t know who to contact in order to claim it. The application process is complicated, and for some there may be stigma attached to claiming.

One solution to lifting more pensioners out of poverty might be increasing the value of pension credit and improving its take-up. It is notable that the triple lock does not apply to pension credit or to winter fuel payments, which use different criteria to work out the rate of increase.

Analysis by the IFS illustrates that the “new” triple lock, as outlined in Burnham’s speech, is still expected to generate an increase in the value of the state pension in the future. However, such increase will not permanently “ratchet up” the level of the state pension in the same way as the “old” triple lock.

articles.title: China and the EU could turn Morocco into a surprise global hub for electric vehicles
articles.author: Linda Calabrese, Senior Research Fellow in the International Economic Development Group, ODI Global
paras: China now makes more than seven in ten of the world’s electric cars. In 2024 it produced over 12 million, 1.25 million of which were exported, mainly to Europe.

The EU is worried about this – alarmed by cheap, state-subsidised Chinese vehicles flooding its market and threatening the 13 million jobs which depend on its own auto industry. So the bloc has spent the past two years building a system of tariffs and rules to keep Chinese cars at bay.
In 2024, it imposed extra duties of up to 35% on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs), on top of an existing 10% import tariff. So far though, the EU’s tactics have yielded limited results.
Chinese vehicle sales in Europe nearly doubled between 2024 and 2025.
And much of this sales volume is being driven by the EV powerhouse that is developing at speed in Morocco.
Chinese firms producing cars in Morocco avoid exposure to those EU tariffs, and have announced US$6 billion (£4.5 billion) of investment in battery and electric car component plants in the country.

As a production base, Morocco has plenty of other advantages too. Its deep-water port in Tangier is the largest in Africa and the Mediterranean. It is also surrounded by state-sponsored industrial zones built specifically for carmakers and their suppliers.
Like its neighbours, Morocco has a free trade agreement with the EU, but is the only north African country which has one with the US.
And crucially, it has a good supply of the critical minerals needed for making batteries for EVs, including around 70% of the world’s phosphate reserves and plenty of cobalt.

Nor is Morocco starting from scratch in the car manufacturing business. Cars are the country’s biggest export. Many Moroccan workers have been trained in automotive assembly thanks to two major car companies.

Renault and Stellantis (the owner of 14 car brands including Peugeot, Fiat and Alfa Romeo) form a manufacturing base in Morocco that exported US$17 billion in cars and parts in 2024. This made Morocco one of the EU’s largest automotive trading partners ahead of China.
Of the 560,000 vehicles Morocco produced in 2024, the vast majority were petrol and diesel models. Only around 50,000 were electric.

But a new wave of investment can help the industry shift to green. Recent multi-billion-euro commitments from Stellantis and Renault will expand EV and hybrid capacity. At the same time, Chinese investment is filling domestic gaps in cathode and battery cell production.
This transformation did not happen to Morocco by chance. The government has spent two decades laying the groundwork.

It has built “free zones”, areas where businesses can import, manufacture, process and re-export goods without paying normal taxes or customs duties. These include automotive “clusters”, including the Tanger “automotive city”.
This year, Morocco introduced a carbon tax to keep its exports compliant with EU rules.
So Morocco has been positioning itself to benefit from the EU tariffs. Whether Morocco actually gains from this boom depends on what kind of production Chinese firms undertake.

They could treat Morocco as a mere transit hub, sending goods through Morocco with minimal processing purely to evade tariffs. Brussels has already caught one such case, ruling in 2025 that aluminium wheels shipped from Morocco were being unfairly subsidised by Beijing.

Or they could do the opposite: build real factories, share technology, train local engineers and buy from Moroccan suppliers. This is what would turn the current boom into lasting green industrialisation, of the type that the African Union wants to encourage, linking African mineral reserves to clean-energy manufacturing.
But there are potential stumbling blocks which could prevent Morocco from benefiting from this new wave of investment in the long term.

First, the EU rules themselves may not last. Its tariffs on Chinese electric cars are set for only five years, and legal challenges are already underway. Second, the technology may remain in Chinese hands. And third, the geopolitical and climate context is so volatile that business plans could change very quickly.

On the plus side, Morocco has an established manufacturing footprint and government support. So the unintended consequences of EU trade policy could end up producing one of the biggest green industrialisation stories of the next decade.
